newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Former strongman Banzer leads polls in Bolivia.
newsitem.headline: Former strongman Banzer leads polls in Bolivia.

text.p: Bolivians go to the polls Sunday in elections likely to return to office Hugo Banzer, a general who still takes pride in crushing leftist guerrillas during his seven years of iron-fisted military rule in the 1970s.
The latest nationwide opinion polls last week show the 71-year-old candidate of the right-wing Nationalist Democratic Alliance (ADN) leading the pack with 25 to 30 percent of the vote.

Former President Jaime Paz Zamora of the Revolutionary Leftist Movement (MIR) is second with 15 to 20 percent. Juan Carlos Duran of the ruling center-right Nationalist Revolutionary Movement (MNR) and Ivo Kuljis of the populist Solidarity Civic Union (UCS) are vying for third place, with Duran slightly ahead.

But no candidate is likely to garner enough ballots to win the Sunday vote in Bolivia, one of the poorest countries in Latin America, and the next leader will be picked by Congress in early August from the top two contenders.
An opinion poll released Friday showed 37 percent of voters in La Paz and nearby El Alto, which together account fot one third of the electorate, are still undecided.

Banzer was asked earlier this week if he would follow the example of the Argentine military, who apologized for human rights abuses during the "Dirty War" against left-wing rebels. He responded: "My conscience is clear. I will not do that."
"There was no room for dialogue in the time that I ruled."

On the economic front, all the major candidates say they will maintain President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada's, free market and privatization drive, the legacy of a harsh austerity program launched in 1985 to halt a price stampede.

Although Bolivia now has single-digit inflation, 70 percent of the population still lives below the poverty line and nearly 40 percent can neither read nor write. The country's per capita output is one tenth that of neighboring Argentina.

Ironically, drugs are not a major campaign issue in Bolivia, which along with Peru and Colombia produces virtually all the world's coca leaf and cocaine, most of which finds its way to the inner-city streets of the United States.

Narcotics mostly come up in relation to Paz Zamora, who has been denied a visa by the White House for his alleged drug-trafficking links. One of Sanchez de Lozada's favorite lines is that if Paz Zamora wins, Bolivia will become an international pariah.

No formal charges have been brought against Paz Zamora, who rejects the accusations. On late Thursday, he showed on television what he said was a U.S. State Department document denying reports that Washington would clamp sanctions on La Paz if he became president.

Although the top candidates have espoused the 12-year-old free-market and privation drive, Banzer says that if he becomes president he will revise the contracts of privatized firms to eliminate their monopolies -- a proposal sure to antagonize the business community.

Since he was ousted in 1978 in one of Bolivia's 190 coups, Banzer has run five times for office. Finally winning the polls in 1985, he failed to garner a strong-enough majority and was defeated in the second round in Congress.

One candidate who has not embraced the free-market drive is Remedios Loza Alvarado, who campaigns in the typical Colla Indian outfit still favored by many in Bolivia, where more than half the population are pure blooded Indians who still uphold the customs and speak the language of their ancestors.
"If you give me your vote, I will rule for Bolivians, not for foreigners," she said in a campaign speech this week.
Although polls show her in fifth place, she could sweep the vote in La Paz, where she has a strong following.
Besides the president and vice-president, whose term will now be five years instead of four, Bolivians will also choose all 27 senators and 130 deputies.
